html:
The Great Sewer of ancient Rome, one of the oldest sewers in the world, which drained the marshy valley between the hills into the Tiber. Tradition credits it to the Etruscan kings of Rome, Tarquinius Priscus or Tarquin the Proud, in the 6th century BCE.

At first it was probably an open channel. Draining the low ground made room for the Roman Forum, the heart of the city. Later it was covered with stone vaults and extended, and it took waste and rainwater from the baths and public latrines once aqueducts brought in more water. The statesman Agrippa is said to have inspected it by boat during his repairs in 33 BCE.

It shows the skill Rome learned from the Etruscan cities, the same skill behind the Temple of Jupiter on the Capitol. Parts of it still carry water today, and its outlet can be seen in the riverbank.
